canonical_topic: Solar panel system sizing and DC-to-AC conversion loss
definition: Solar panels natively produce DC power, which must pass through an inverter to become grid-usable AC power; this conversion (plus other system losses) typically discards about a quarter of the generated energy.
core_idea: Because panels are rated in either AC or DC terms, and inverter capacity caps how much DC can be converted, actual grid-delivered AC output is meaningfully lower than nameplate DC production.
key_points: An inverter is required to convert panel DC output into grid-compatible AC power.
There is a maximum conversion capacity set by inverter size; a bigger inverter raises system output but adds installation cost.
Total system losses (conversion plus other losses) are typically around 25 percent.
Example given: 1 KW of DC production yields roughly 0.75 KW of AC power delivered to the grid.
relationships: Explains why nameplate DC capacity differs from realized AC capacity used in capacity factor calculations.
trading_implications: System sizing decisions trade inverter cost against captured AC output, since inverter capacity — not panel DC rating — caps deliverable power.
caveats: A panel's DC rating is not what reaches the grid; roughly 25% is lost by the time power is delivered as AC.
